title: Adab of speech
hookLine: say good or keep silent: the manners of the tongue start in the gap before a word

cards: A reply sits half typed. The cursor blinks. It's sharp, it's accurate, and it would land.
Your thumb hovers over send. Between the thought and the word there's a gap about one breath wide, and a lot happens in it.
The manners of speech in Islam begin right there, with a short line from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. It ties the way a person talks to faith itself, and it offers exactly two choices.
Neither of them is the sharp reply.

teach.b: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good, or keep silent.
It opens with belief, as if speech is where faith shows up in public. Then it gives two doors, and only two. Good, or silent.
There's no third door marked true, so I'll say it anyway. The Qur'an raises the bar.
In al-Isra, in Pickthall's translation: "Tell My bondmen to speak that which is kindlier." Not only kind. Kindlier: of two true things, the gentler one.
And in al-Baqarah, among the duties of a covenant: "speak kindly to mankind." Mankind, not only friends. Words don't simply vanish, either.
Surah Qaf says of each person: "He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready."
Tradition says that observer is an angel who records; some readers take the verse less as a threat than as a reason to slow down. This is the filter that comes before backbiting and lying.

teach.h: SILENCE AS A CHOICE, NOT A HIDING.
teach.b: And so the hadith isn't misheard: silence doesn't mean swallowing the truth when it's needed. The Qur'an also calls believers to stand firm for justice, as witnesses for Allah, even against themselves.
The silence here is chosen: the word you could have said, left unsaid, because it wasn't good. Courtesy, held in the mouth.

how: Muslim teachers cite the hadith "say good or keep silent" when they teach the manners of speech, often alongside the Qur'an's call to speak the kindlier word.

o: always say what's true, however it lands
keep silent about every wrong you see
say what is good, or keep silent

games.q: the adab of speech — tap the pairs.
p: an observer ready for every word

s: the hadith opens with a rule about words
it opens with belief: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day.
the Qur'an asks for the kindlier word, not only a true one
al-Isra: tell My bondmen to speak that which is kindlier.
keeping silent means never speaking up
the Qur'an also calls believers to stand firm for justice, even against themselves.

games.q: a friend shares something they're proud of. you spot a flaw and have a sharp, accurate comment ready. by today's hadith, what are your doors?
o: the sharp comment, because it's true.
say it to someone else instead.
games.why: the hadith gives two doors only: say what is good, or keep silent. true, so I'll say it anyway isn't one of them.

practice: Bring to mind one conversation coming up, or one message waiting for a reply, and hear the first thing you'd say. Hold it at the two doors: is it good, and if not, can it become kindlier, or stay unsaid?
Breathe in and notice the word, breathe out and let it wait; if you pray, you can hold the words speak that which is kindlier in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Adab of speech. The manners of the tongue: say what is good or keep silent, and of two true words, choose the kindlier. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "let him keep silent," the hadith's second door.

carryVoice: Your line: good, or silent. Of two true words, the kindlier. Tomorrow, the adab of eating.
